statement: A straight tunnel is bored through the center of a uniform Earth (surface gravity $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$) and an object is dropped in. Find the period of the resulting oscillation, in seconds.
solution: Inside a uniform sphere the field is $g r/R$, a restoring force proportional to displacement, so the motion is simple harmonic with $\omega^2 = g/R$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} = 5.06\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$, about 84 minutes: the same as a low orbit.

name: Binary star period
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Two stars of mass $2.0\times 10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg}$ each orbit their common center of mass, with a separation of $1.0\times 10^{12}\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the orbital period, in seconds.
solution: Each star circles at radius $d/2$ with the full separation setting the force: $GM^2/d^2 = M4\pi^2(d/2)/T^2$. This rearranges to $T = 2\pi\sqrt{d^3/(G(M_1+M_2))} = 3.85\times 10^8\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Change in g with altitude
statement: Earth has radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ and surface gravity $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the decrease in $g$ at an altitude of $10\;\mathrm{km}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For $h \ll R$, $g(h) \approx g(1-2h/R)$, so $\Delta g \approx 2gh/R = 2(9.81)(10^4)/(6.37\times 10^6) = 0.0308\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. A commercial airliner's altitude changes weight by only about $0.3\%$.

name: Extra speed to escape from orbit
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius $7.0\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the additional speed it must gain to escape Earth entirely, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Circular speed is $\sqrt{GM/r} = 7545\;\mathrm{m/s}$ and escape speed at the same radius is $\sqrt2$ times that, $10670\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The difference is $3.13\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Field off the axis of two masses
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Two $1.00\times 10^3\;\mathrm{kg}$ spheres sit $2.00\;\mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the magnitude of the gravitational field at a point $1.00\;\mathrm{m}$ from the midpoint, on the perpendicular bisector, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Each sphere is $\sqrt2\;\mathrm{m}$ away, contributing $GM/r^2 = 3.34\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The components along the bisector add and the perpendicular ones cancel, so the total is $2(3.34\times 10^{-8})\cos 45^\circ = 4.72\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Leaving the solar system
statement: Earth orbits the Sun at $2.978\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Ignoring Earth's own gravity, find the speed a probe at Earth's orbital radius needs to escape the Sun, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: For a circular orbit the escape speed at that radius is $\sqrt2$ times the orbital speed, since $v_{esc}^2 = 2GM/r = 2v_{circ}^2$. So $v = \sqrt2(2.978\times 10^4) = 4.21\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Falling from two Earth radii
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. An object is released from rest at a distance of two Earth radii from Earth's center. Find its speed on reaching the surface (ignore the atmosphere), in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Energy conservation with the correct $1/r$ potential gives $\tfrac12v^2 = GM(1/R - 1/2R) = GM/2R$. Then $v = \sqrt{GM/R} = 7.91\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Using a constant $g$ over that distance would be badly wrong.

name: Speeding up as a satellite decays
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Atmospheric drag lowers a satellite's circular orbit from $300\;\mathrm{km}$ to $200\;\mathrm{km}$ altitude. Find the increase in its orbital speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Orbital speed is $\sqrt{GM/r}$, so it grows as the orbit shrinks: $7784$ vs $7726\;\mathrm{m/s}$, an increase of $58\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Drag removes energy yet the satellite ends up moving faster, because the potential energy drops by twice as much as the kinetic energy gains.

name: Third law with AU and years
statement: An asteroid orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of $4.00\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.
solution: In these units Kepler's third law is simply $T^2 = a^3$. So $T = 4^{3/2} = 8.00\;\mathrm{years}$.

name: Working backward to the radius
statement: A comet orbits the Sun with a period of $27.0\;\mathrm{years}$. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.

name: Period of Mars
statement: Mars orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of $1.524\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.
solution: $T = a^{3/2} = 1.524^{3/2} = 1.881\;\mathrm{years}$, close to the observed value of about 687 days.

name: Distance of Jupiter
statement: Jupiter takes $11.86\;\mathrm{years}$ to orbit the Sun. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.

name: Doubling the orbit radius
statement: Satellite B orbits Earth in a circle of exactly twice the radius of satellite A's orbit. Find the ratio of B's period to A's period.
solution: Since $T \propto a^{3/2}$, the ratio is $2^{3/2} = 2.83$.

name: Four times the radius
statement: A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $r$ to one of radius $4r$. Find the factor by which its period increases.
solution: $T \propto a^{3/2}$, so the factor is $4^{3/2} = 8.00$.

name: Halley's comet
statement: Halley's comet has a semi-major axis of $17.8\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.

name: Semi-major axis from the extremes
statement: A comet's closest approach to the Sun is $0.60\;\mathrm{AU}$ and its farthest distance is $5.40\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.
solution: The semi-major axis is the average of perihelion and aphelion: $a = (0.60+5.40)/2 = 3.00\;\mathrm{AU}$. Then $T = 3^{3/2} = 5.20\;\mathrm{years}$.

name: Eccentricity of Earth's orbit
statement: Earth's perihelion distance is $0.983\;\mathrm{AU}$ and its aphelion distance is $1.017\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find the eccentricity of its orbit.
solution: With $r_p = a(1-e)$ and $r_a = a(1+e)$, $e = (r_a-r_p)/(r_a+r_p) = 0.034/2.000 = 0.017$. Earth's orbit is very nearly circular.

name: Equal areas at the two ends
statement: A comet moves at $5.0\;\mathrm{km/s}$ at aphelion, which is four times farther from the Sun than its perihelion. Find its perihelion speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: At the two extremes the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so the second law gives $r_pv_p = r_av_a$. Then $v_p = 4(5.0\;\mathrm{km/s}) = 2.0\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Period of Ceres
statement: Ceres orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of $2.77\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.

name: Third law in SI units
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$. Find the period of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $1.00\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$, in seconds.
solution: Kepler's third law in SI form is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM}$. With $a^3 = 10^{21}\;\mathrm{m^3}$ and $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}$, $T = 9.96\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: The Kepler constant for the Sun
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and a solar mass of $1.99\times 10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg}$. Find the value of $T^2/a^3$ for objects orbiting the Sun, in $\mathrm{s^2/m^3}$.
solution: Kepler's third law says this ratio is the same for every orbit, and equals $4\pi^2/GM = 39.48/(1.327\times 10^{20}) = 2.98\times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{s^2/m^3}$.

name: Mass of a binary system
statement: Two stars orbit each other with a period of $50.0\;\mathrm{years}$ and a separation of $20.0\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find their combined mass, in solar masses.
solution: In solar units the third law generalizes to $a^3/T^2 = M_{total}$. So $M = 8000/2500 = 3.20$ solar masses.

name: Perihelion speed from vis-viva
statement: A comet has a semi-major axis of $2.00\;\mathrm{AU}$ and eccentricity $0.500$. Take $1\;\mathrm{AU} = 1.496\times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}$ and $GM_{Sun} = 1.327\times 10^{20}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. Find its speed at perihelion, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Perihelion is at $a(1-e) = 1.00\;\mathrm{AU}$. The vis-viva equation $v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a)$ gives $v^2 = 1.327\times 10^{20}(1.337\times 10^{-11} - 3.34\times 10^{-12})$, so $v = 3.65\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Aphelion speed of the same comet
statement: For the same comet ($a = 2.00\;\mathrm{AU}$, $e = 0.500$, $GM_{Sun} = 1.327\times 10^{20}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $1\;\mathrm{AU} = 1.496\times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}$), find its speed at aphelion, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Aphelion is at $a(1+e) = 3.00\;\mathrm{AU}$. Vis-viva gives $v = 1.22\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$, exactly one third of the perihelion speed as the second law requires.

name: Geostationary orbit from lunar data
statement: The Moon orbits Earth at a radius of $3.84\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $27.32\;\mathrm{days}$. Find the radius of an Earth orbit with a period of $1.00\;\mathrm{day}$, in meters.
solution: Kepler's third law applies to anything orbiting Earth, so $a = a_{Moon}(T/T_{Moon})^{2/3} = 3.84\times 10^8(1/27.32)^{2/3} = 4.22\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$. No knowledge of $G$ or Earth's mass is needed.

name: Weighing Mars with Phobos
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Phobos orbits Mars at a radius of $9.38\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $7.65\;\mathrm{hours}$. Find the mass of Mars, in kilograms.
solution: Rearrange the third law: $M = 4\pi^2a^3/(GT^2)$ with $T = 2.754\times 10^4\;\mathrm{s}$. That gives $M = 6.44\times 10^{23}\;\mathrm{kg}$.

name: Areal velocity of Earth
statement: Treat Earth's orbit as a circle of radius $1.496\times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $3.156\times 10^7\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the rate at which the Sun-Earth line sweeps out area, in $\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
solution: The second law says this rate is constant, so it is just the total area over the period: $\pi r^2/T = \pi(1.496\times 10^{11})^2/(3.156\times 10^7) = 2.23\times 10^{15}\;\mathrm{m^2/s}$.

name: Aphelion of an asteroid
statement: An asteroid has an orbital period of $5.00\;\mathrm{years}$ and a perihelion distance of $1.20\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its aphelion distance, in AU.
solution: The third law gives $a = 5^{2/3} = 2.924\;\mathrm{AU}$. Since $r_p + r_a = 2a$, the aphelion is $2(2.924) - 1.20 = 4.65\;\mathrm{AU}$.

name: Period of an elliptical Earth orbit
statement: Use $GM_E = 3.983\times 10^{14}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. A satellite has perigee radius $6.70\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ and apogee radius $4.20\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$. Find its orbital period, in seconds.
solution: The semi-major axis is $a = (6.70\times 10^6 + 4.20\times 10^7)/2 = 2.435\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM} = 3.78\times 10^4\;\mathrm{s}$, about 10.5 hours.

name: Perigee speed
statement: For the same satellite (perigee $6.70\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$, apogee $4.20\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$, $GM_E = 3.983\times 10^{14}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$), find its speed at perigee, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Vis-viva with $a = 2.435\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$: $v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a) = 3.983\times 10^{14}(2.574\times 10^{-7})$, so $v = 1.01\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Hohmann transfer to Mars
statement: A spacecraft leaves Earth's orbit ($1.00\;\mathrm{AU}$) on an ellipse whose aphelion just touches Mars's orbit ($1.524\;\mathrm{AU}$). Find the travel time from Earth to Mars, in years.
solution: The transfer ellipse has $a = (1.00+1.524)/2 = 1.262\;\mathrm{AU}$, so its full period is $1.262^{3/2} = 1.418\;\mathrm{years}$. The trip is half an orbit: $0.709\;\mathrm{years}$, about 8.5 months.

name: Speed ratio for a very eccentric orbit
statement: A comet has eccentricity $0.900$. Find the ratio of its perihelion speed to its aphelion speed.
solution: The second law gives $r_pv_p = r_av_a$, and $r_a/r_p = (1+e)/(1-e)$. So $v_p/v_a = 1.9/0.1 = 19.0$.

name: Orbits per day
statement: Use $GM_E = 3.983\times 10^{14}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and Earth's radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A satellite orbits at an altitude of $700\;\mathrm{km}$. Find how many complete orbits it makes in one day ($86400\;\mathrm{s}$).
solution: With $r = 7.07\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM} = 5.92\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$. Then $86400/5920 = 14.6$ orbits per day.

name: Apogee of a fast launch
statement: Use $GM_E = 3.983\times 10^{14}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and Earth's radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A projectile is launched horizontally from the surface at $9000\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the maximum distance it reaches from Earth's center, in meters.
solution: The launch point is the perigee. Energy and angular momentum conservation give $r_a = r_p/(2GM/(r_pv_p^2)-1)$. With $2GM/(r_pv_p^2) = 1.544$, $r_a = 6.37\times 10^6/0.544 = 1.17\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Mass of a galactic center
statement: A star orbits the center of a galaxy with a semi-major axis of $1000\;\mathrm{AU}$ and a period of $15.0\;\mathrm{years}$. Find the mass of the central object, in solar masses.
solution: Using $M = a^3/T^2$ in solar units, $M = 10^9/225 = 4.44\times 10^6$ solar masses. The star's own mass is negligible in comparison.

name: Period depends only on density
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Find the period of a circular orbit skimming the surface of a uniform sphere of density $5500\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, in seconds.
solution: Writing $M = \tfrac43\pi R^3\rho$ in $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R^3/GM}$ makes $R$ cancel: $T = \sqrt{3\pi/G\rho}$. That gives $T = \sqrt{2.57\times 10^7} = 5.07\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$, the same 84 minutes as low Earth orbit.

name: Falling straight into the Sun
statement: Earth is imagined stopped in its orbit and released, so it falls radially toward the Sun. Treating the radial fall as a degenerate ellipse of semi-major axis $0.500\;\mathrm{AU}$, find the time to reach the Sun, in days.
solution: A straight-line fall is the limit of an ellipse with $a = r_0/2$, and reaching the center is half of that orbit. So $t = \tfrac12(0.5)^{3/2}\;\mathrm{yr} = 0.1768\;\mathrm{yr} = 64.6\;\mathrm{days}$.

name: Burn to raise the apogee
statement: Use $GM_E = 3.983\times 10^{14}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. A satellite in a circular orbit of radius $7.00\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ fires its engine to enter an ellipse with apogee $4.20\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the required change in speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The circular speed is $\sqrt{GM/r} = 7545\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The transfer ellipse has $a = 2.45\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$, and vis-viva gives a perigee speed of $9876\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The burn must add $2.33\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$.
